utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We are here to continue our sitting in this case and simply for the transcript, I turn towards the Prosecutor. We all know each other very well, but still.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. If you please, my name is Mr. Niemann, I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda and Mr. Marchesiello and Ms. Erasmus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Mr. Mikulicic and I appear together with my colleague, Mr. Joka, on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that we can continue with yesterday's witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, I would like to give an indication to your Honours at this stage in the proceedings of witnesses that we have left available this week. At the moment, we anticipate having available for the continuation of the week eight witnesses. We do not think that will be enough to consume the full time that we have available. I might indicate that we started off with a list of 24 and that has been depleted savagely to at least half of that, by a variety of reasons, but that is what we are left with despite our best endeavours. I think we will proceed, probably with a full witness list, until Thursday. Then Thursday I think we may only have one witness on Thursday and on Friday we may only have two. I indicate that at this stage, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Will the testimonies be completed by Friday morning, Mr. Prosecutor? Will we have finished with the witnesses by then, that you have indicated for this week, because the Trial Chamber cannot sit on Friday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see, yes. Well, we can probably accommodate that, your Honours, if your Honours cannot sit Friday afternoon. That would be convenient from our point of view. We will have further witnesses in the next section. We tried to bring -- there is a week in March, at the end of March, which we tried to bring some of those witnesses forward but we just cannot achieve that, unfortunately. We will still be calling evidence in this week. This is eight witnesses for this week, it will conclude all the witnesses we intended to call and we will keep in mind that your Honours are not available on Friday afternoon. I think that will now make it that we will be able to be kept busy for the whole time, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That is fine, Mr. Niemann. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is brought in, can we bring down the curtains?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you pull down the curtains, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness H.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are going to continue to hear your testimony. I should like to remind you that yesterday you took a solemn oath, according to which you told us that you would tell us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Are you now in the same state of mind for us to be able to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are now going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor, please. WITNESS H (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, your Honours. Good morning, learned colleagues, good morning, Witness H. My name is Mr. Mikulicic, I am Defence counsel for the accused in this case. I am now going to ask you a number of questions and I should kindly ask you to answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. H, do you recall whether, about the middle of April 1993, there was any fighting in the vicinity of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall with precision, but there was fighting quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far from your village was the fighting, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly about a kilometre or maybe even less away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, that is very close.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but it was advancing towards the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. H, at the time, were you a civilian or a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the army, but I was wearing civilian clothes and I was registered as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say you were registered as a civilian, you are referring to your registration in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. H, when you were describing yesterday the events in your village, when soldiers in camouflage uniform came, you said that some of those soldiers were from Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you please tell them, were the people from Herzegovina, are they from Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is Herzegovina a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and I hope it will continue to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. H, were you registered when you arrived in Kaonik, and by whom? You just told us that you were registered as a civilian, by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did the International Red Cross come in relation to your arrival at Kaonik, how many days later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly the number of days that went by. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that there were battles in the vicinity, in the village; when these soldiers came to your village, what were they looking for in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were looking for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. H, you described to us yesterday that actually in the first half of 1993, in the area where you were living, there were two conflicts: there was one at the beginning of the year and another somewhere in April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the area where you were residing, let us not mention that area, in the first half of 1993, there were two conflicts; that is one at the beginning of the year in January and another one in April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were in between these two conflicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday that during the first conflict, I was at home and during the cease-fire I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, between the two conflicts, you were in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you in any way involved in civil defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone from your village participated in the work of the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but, as far as I know, there was no organisation after the first conflict, as far as I can recollect. I am not quite sure again, because I was not involved in any of the more important organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. H, were you a member of any political party in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your village had a mixed population, if I am not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, there were Bosniak Croats and Bosniak Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us, if you know, what the share of each group was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, because I never counted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you cannot even tell us roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be better for me not to answer the question than to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That, you are probably right. You told us yesterday, Mr. H, that during your stay in Kaonik you noticed that some elderly and sick people were released home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not home, but to the village of Skradno. These were elderly men and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many men were there, could you tell us, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about 30. Something like that, I do not know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in the camp like the others and during my stay there they were released to the village of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. H, let us go back to the day when a person fled, escaped from Kaonik. You described the event for us yesterday, as far as you were able to remember it. I just have a couple of questions in that connection, for the sake of clarification. How many people, including this person that escaped, were outside the building? I think you said they were planting potatoes; how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a total of four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many guards were watching over those four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Miro Maric took them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But how much people were outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see because I was in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. You were in cell number what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was with you in cell number 16, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, but I would not like to name the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But let us make it clear, do you not wish to name them because you do not wish to do it or because we are now in an open session and you do not want to cause any embarrassment to those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I then ask the Trial Chamber to go into private session, as names may appear in the testimony which need to be protected? If the Prosecutor agrees, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I fully agree to my learned friend's application to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Let us now go into private session. Is the audio visual department ready?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I should like to ask the usher to show Witness H a picture which has already been admitted as Prosecutor's Exhibit P54. (Handed). Thank you. Could the technicians move the projector so that we can see the whole photograph, please? Thank you. Mr. H, yesterday, describing this photograph, you marked the building with the letters A and B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what was the function of the other buildings that we can see on this photograph; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the building which is in the upper third of the photograph was used for? Next to the road. Do you see that building? Could you point to it? That is the building I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was where most of the soldiers were. When we prisoners were going out, there were some soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO army. That is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I was a prisoner. Aleksovski knows that best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. H, it is now you that are answering the questions. If you do not know the answer, say that you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from my answer you can tell that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. H, do you know where the four persons you were telling us about, who were planting potatoes, where they were doing that? Could you show us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, let us summarise: the building I was referring to, would you please mark it with the letter C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that the HVO army was accommodated there. Are you aware whether that building was used as part of the Kaonik prisoners? Were prisoners put there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I stayed in these two other buildings. I do not know about the other people, I mostly saw the military there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, was this building part of the Kaonik compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the closest building to the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. H, yesterday you said that Zlatko Aleksovski -- and I quote your words -- was "a commander of all forces within the barracks compound"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, that is your opinion. Is it also your opinion that Zlatko Aleksovski was also the commander of all forces that were stationed in the building C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that, but most probably. I think I already said that this is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you have a reason for such an opinion which you could share with us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the way he introduced himself. He said that he was Zlatko Aleksovski and that he was the warden of the entire prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, in your opinion, he was also the commander of the forces which was in the building C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I told you that I made a difference between a warden and a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. H, I will rephrase my question: in your opinion, was Zlatko Aleksovski also the commander of the military which was in building C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot say that -- you could say that he was also a warden that also was in control of the military there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. H, you saw the soldiers in this building C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them around the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, around the building. Did you see that these soldiers had different kinds of uniforms than the other soldiers around, and I would like to draw your attention to the belts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice that, but I noticed several times that they wore shorts and T-shirts, so that I thought this is what they use for relaxing and rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you also see them wearing white belts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only noticed soldiers wearing white belts at the gate and around that building there were different soldiers, but for the most part they were just regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. H, I only have one additional question: after the escape which we discussed, you said that you heard some moans coming from other cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see that anyone was beating anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say that I heard it, it does not mean that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So would it be correct if I said that you did not see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no further questions. Thank you. Excuse me, just one additional question. It slipped my mind and my colleague just reminded me of it. Mr. H, I will put this question to you in the following way: after all these difficult experiences, would a witness before court in a criminal case in -- were you a witness in a criminal case in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I was called before a court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you gave a statement there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you testified before a superior court in Zenica; was it also true that you also asked for damages at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not my idea, it was a judge's idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So what did you tell this judge? How much in damages did you ask for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that it is not myself who asked for damages, that it was the suggestion of the judge and I was not hoping for any, and he said that he -- he advised me that I could ask for damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So can you tell me how much you asked for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not my request, it was his request. I do not know. I only know that I gave the same kind of a statement, but I know that underneath the statement, he put some number as the amount of damage that I could be entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have before me a report and I would like permission to show it to the witness so that the witness can identify it as the statement that he had given there and that it is the statement that he had signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I have a copy of the statement which my learned friend is seeking to show to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: May the Prosecution be given a copy of that statement which my learned friend is now seeking to show the witness, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, can the Prosecution have a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, there is no problem in the Prosecution getting a copy of it. Right now I only have a single copy, so in the next break I will make a copy and give it to the Prosecution, if that is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In any event, before showing it to the witness, can you please show it to Mr. Meddegoda. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I wonder whether the document has been translated or whether it is in the Bosnian language or whether it is translated into one of the official languages of this court, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document in question has not been translated because I did not know that I will be in a position to use it in cross-examination. However, if the Defence is allowed to use it in its own case, then it will be translated. However, at this stage we would just like the witness to identify his own signature and a portion of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, I think this is a question only of identification of the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour. In any event, may I see the statement, your Honours? (Handed). Thank you. (Pause). Very well, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Meddegoda, are you asking for the document to be entered into the record, or is it sufficient for the witness to see the document and identify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: My learned friend is showing this document to the witness. It is a Defence document, your Honour. We have no objection to the document being marked for the purposes of identification of the signature, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Mikulicic, the document can be admitted into the record. Are we agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence agrees, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you can continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interrupt at this stage. My learned friend is seeking to show this document only for the purpose of identification of the signature of this witness. If the document is admitted only for that limited purpose, I think, your Honours, the Prosecution has no objection to such admission; only for the limited purpose of identification of the signature, as my learned friend is seeking to elicit at this very moment, your Honours. The document is not translated and has not been provided to the Prosecution before. Therefore, for that reason, I respectfully urge that your Honours be pleased to admit the document only for the purposes of identification of the witness's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I beg your pardon, your aim is simply to show the witness his signature on the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my objective is to show the signature on the document and ask the witness to authenticate it, if it be possible, and also for him to authenticate a portion of the text relating to the damages request on page 3. If we are allowed to translate that portion of the document on page 3, this is actually the objective of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That was what I was going to suggest to you. You can put the document under the ELMO; you can read the document and it will be translated to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, regarding the content. Are you all in agreement? We are going to put the document under the ELMO. Mr. Mikulicic will read the document, it will be translated. In that way, we will be familiarised with its contents; is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The Defence agrees with it and it is a very short paragraph on page 3 of the statement that is in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honour is aware of the Prosecution's position. Your Honours have ruled that the document should be admitted in that way. The Prosecution has no objection to your Honours' ruling on that, but the Prosecution position is that the document has not been provided to it before and it has not been provided with the translation of the document and that the Prosecution is unaware of the authenticity of the document which is now being produced, which my learned friend is seeking to produce before your Honour's court. The Prosecution will go along with the ruling your Honour made on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, the Trial Chamber has decided to admit the document by placing it under the ELMO and read by Mr. Mikulicic. This will be an element of the testimony, but not an official document. Therefore, Mr. Mikulicic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. H, I think we should go into the private session since we can see the name of the witness on the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The witness is protected and I think we must go in closed session because we are going to see his signature. Therefore, we are now going into closed session. Is that possible, or private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It would be preferable to have a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: A closed session, thank you very much, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Meddegoda, have you any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No questions in re-examination, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meddegoda. Witness H, I have a question for you: in your culture, in your language, and even in a situation of conflict that you lived through, a commander and a director; are they one and the same, or are they two different words to express a different reality? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In my opinion, a director or warden is a civilian with such duty and such a post and the commander would be a military person. From what I know, this was a military installation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And how did Mr. Aleksovski introduce himself to you; as a director or as a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He introduced himself as a warden of the prison, Zlatko Aleksovski, but his soldiers in the compound addressed him as "Mr. Commander".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: When he introduced himself was he in civilian clothes or camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In civilian clothes. Later on he also wore both the camouflage uniform and civilian clothes. He often went to Busovaca, I do not know for what purpose, but he was for the most part within the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness H. You have completed your testimony. The International Criminal Tribunal thanks you for coming. We wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. The next witness is Mr. Garanovic Rasim. He did not ask for any protective measures, so he will be taken and he will answer our questions with his real name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: May I ask the court, how much time shall we have before the interruption, so to choose when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The break is envisaged for 11.20 am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I am afraid this is the wrong witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor. Could we have the break now, perhaps. Then you can regulate everything in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: That is what I suggest too. It would be a very good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The interpreters in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, we will have the break and we will resume at 11.20. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Before beginning, or rather resuming, it should be said that the document that we discussed is going to be admitted into the record, under which number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit D2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: This was an exceptional situation because, as you know, Article 3 of the Rules requires documents to be translated into official languages. For the moment, this document was only partly translated, but this is really going to be an exception. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I think we are now ready to have Mr. Garanovic. I hope it will be the right witness this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. You are going to read the declaration given to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated. What is your name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Rasim Garanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garanovic, for coming. You are going to answer the questions that the Prosecutor is going to put to you. RASIM GARANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Garanovic. May I ask you to state --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: May I ask you to state, again, your full name, age, date and place of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Rasim Garanovic. Born on 7th May 1950 in the village of Serici, municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What is then your nationality and your faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak by nationality. My ethnic origin is Muslim and my religion is Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What is your job, Mr. Garanovic? What was your job in the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a professional stone-cutter. I processed stone and marble, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you have workers under your -- at your disposal that worked with you and under you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How many of them and of which nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes there were more, sometimes less workers. But as a rule, I had five workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And in April 1993, did you have five workers under you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How many of them were Croats and how many Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two were Muslims and three were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were there, at that time, or had there been at that time problems as to these two different ethnicities within the same context working, the same context and the same situation of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question very well. Are you referring to the place where we were living, whether there were any problems among the different inhabitants, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I am referring both to the place in general and the situation that was existing in your shop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no problems at all. Actually, we all lived in harmony. My village of Krcevine, a village near the town of Vitez, it was inhabited mostly by Croats and Muslims, Bosniaks. Ninety per cent of the population were Croats, 10 per cent were Bosniaks. We lived together; we rejoiced together. We worked together, we helped each other in various activities. We built our homes together, our roads, telephone lines, we celebrated our religious holidays, Christmas, Bajram, all of us together, really together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did something in this situation that you are describing, did something start changing and how is it -- did things change actually in the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993, things started to change. Something strange began to happen. Simply I do not know where from, most probably from Zagreb. The Croats were given a sign telling them that they were in jeopardy, and through the HVO, the HVO police, they started to ignore their neighbours, Bosniaks. They had less and less contact with the Bosniaks and those who wanted to communicate with them did not dare do that for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were there HVO forces in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was a checkpoint right next to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, let us go to the 14th April 1993. What happened to you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th April, I came early from Zenica. I went there to see a doctor, my doctor, and I had to be close to a doctor and he was in Zenica, but I had to go on a business trip, to Jablanica, which is about 120 kilometres from Vitez in Herzegovina. In the morning, my wife and I got into our car, we reached our company in Vitez, next to the flat where we lived in. With a worker of mine, I started off on the trip to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was this worker a Croat and what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this worker was a Croat. His name was Ratko Strukar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened on your way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started off before 7.00 in the morning, about 6.45 in the morning, or maybe 6.40, I am not quite sure. We got as far as Stojkovici, which is a suburb of Novi Travnik. We noticed a large number of trucks there, that were parked in an unusual manner. Then there were many passenger vehicles which were open as well. There were small children crying in those cars. In some cars the parents were there not and it struck us as a strange situation. The police stopped us there, the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked for our ID cards, our identification papers. We showed them. We had passes issued by the HVO and the BiH army, giving us permission to go on this business trip. We showed them all this, I and my worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Nevertheless, were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They immediately said: "Get out. You are arrested", and they told my worker to go back where he had come from, which meant to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who were those who arrested you? In which kind of insignia, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniforms, with HVO insignia. It was the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where were you taken after having been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me about 300 metres to the right, to a military warehouse which used to be the warehouse of the Yugoslav army. That was where an airport, a military airport was to be built, and this warehouse was built for that purpose. They took me there to this warehouse, to the warehouse compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where did they put you into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a kind of container. They opened it and they put me in the container. The container was partitioned. It is the kind of container that is loaded on to trucks. There was a partition of about 1 metre 30 and that is where they shut me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you alone in the container -- in that area of the container?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At the time there were several men there. I did not count, but in my estimate there were at least 15, at least 15 persons there. They simply pushed us in. We were standing next to one another, face-to-face, we could hardly breathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that container, in that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed there in that situation from 7.00 in the morning until the evening, about nightfall, when they took out some people. I do not know where they took them. Several men were taken out, so that we had a little more space. So we could sit in between each other's legs and sleep a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You said that you had been visiting a doctor in Zenica. What were your physical conditions at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had undergone surgery in April 1992, in Belgrade. I operated my stomach and oesophagus. My physical condition was very serious, due to the consequences of the operation. That is why I took my worker to accompany me, for him to drive and to help me on the business trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, can you describe what subsequently happened to you and how you were transported away from that area to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there on the 14th. There was no conflict there at the time, there were no military operations. They arrested us there, they shut us up about 7.00 in the morning, that is me. We stayed there the 14th and then the 15th until the evening. On the 15th, in the morning, they gave us something to eat. There was something -- a kind of lunch package received through charity organisations. Then they ordered all those with trucks -- that is the drivers -- and whose trucks had stayed behind on the road, to come out. Then they did get out these drivers, several minutes later they drove those trucks into the compound. These were trucks loaded with goods, mostly food stuffs, or they were on their way to collect goods, either in Croatia or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, let us return to your personal situation. What happened to you and your fellows on the morning of April 15th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 15th April, that is what I am talking about now, they took us out of the container around 10.00. They took us in front of a shed and the HVO police were there. They required statements from us, that is to tell them where we were going, who we were, what we were doing, why we were travelling, why we were going where we were. Then when that was over, they took us back to the container and we stayed there until nightfall. Late in the evening -- I do not know what time it was, I really do not know , we were in such a situation that we did not know -- the buses came. I saw two buses there when I came out. This was the HVO police who had called us to come out, to get out of the container and to raise our hands, lean them against the bus for them to search us. They searched us. They did not seize our personal belongings, only if someone had a knife or something like that. They ordered us to get into the bus. We got into this first bus that I got into and I sat down. The buses started towards the gates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, please, if you could go to the moment which will probably be most interesting for us, when you did arrive at Kaonik. Will you describe the arrival of the buses in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to allow me to go back just for a second to the 14th, if possible, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No, go ahead, if you do not mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started with the buses towards the gates, then the buses went further on. I knew roughly, or I assumed where they were taking us, to a camp probably, some sort of a camp. I was afraid that we might turn right because turning right meant going to Herzegovina. Fortunately, we went left, which meant towards Vitez. The buses went as far as the cross-roads known as "Okuka", or "the bend", and I saw a checkpoint there held by the Croat army. They had RPGs facing the bus and other inventory weapons. We passed that checkpoint and turned right. We passed through Vitez and from there on to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I think you have a very good memory of those events, and I understand the reason for this. Now I would like you to concentrate on the camp, on the moment you did arrive to the camp. You spoke -- can I introduce as evidence, the aerial photograph you already know, of the camp? Can I have it shown to the witness, please? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you put it on the ELMO, please? Thank you. Now, Mr. Garanovic, do you recognise the camp where you have been taken with the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the camp where we were taken with the buses. The buses came along this road, they got to here, then they turned right. This is the road to Busovaca. Turned right. There is a military barracks here. (Indicating on photograph). Then they went on towards this wood --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? You mentioned before the gates of the camp; were there gates and where were they, at the entrance? Was there a gate to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were waiting there for the gates to be opened. There was a gate, but it was night-time, so it was about midnight by the time we got there. We did not see that too well. I cannot describe the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got there, along this road. (Indicating on photograph). They drove us to this hangar here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you put a circle around it and mark it with the letter "A", please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They brought us here, the buses stopped. The bus stopped, the one I was in. It stopped in front of the building, about the middle of the building. There is about -- about the middle of the building, there is an entrance into the hangar, so we entered. The light was very poor. The HVO policemen -- the police told us immediately to go up to the wall, the length of the building -- that is the other side of the entrance -- to raise our hands up, to lean them against the wall and to stay there. Nobody should move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You refer to HVO police; were they policemen or military, according to your experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was both policemen and HVO military. They did not differ very much anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How did they differ, if there was any difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not differ in terms of their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: But in terms of their attire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO police, those who were policemen, had the word written on it, "police". Those who were soldiers had just the HVO insignia. There at the entrance to the right, as we were passing, I noticed a pile and I did not really know what it was at first. It was quite dark. To the right here -- actually those were people who had been brought there before us, so we must have been a second group to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Were they and were you all civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all civilians, until the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You did not see any BiH military held as prisoner in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see -- at that time I did not see them. These were all civilians, who later told me that they were working their fields and that the HVO soldiers arrived, or the police, that they rounded them up and took them from the fields to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long were you forced to stay standing up with your hands raised against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A very long time. That was very difficult. It was cold. I was cold, I was very cold. My hands were cold from that wall. It was also some kind of weapons depot from the JNA. We stood there for maybe 40 minutes, more or less. These people over there were discussing something, I think it had to do with the organisation. Then they ordered that all our personal belongings, everything -- even a small piece of paper could cost your life, if you did not produce it and if you did not place it next to your feet. So, indeed, all my personal belongings, I was afraid that something would stay on me, so I placed all these things next to my right foot and when we did this, they told us to place our hands against a wall again, facing the wall, which is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were your belongings given back to you after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At that moment -- partially, yes. At that moment the HVO soldiers came. They took the belongings, the money, gold, if anybody had rings, watches, valuables. As far as I am concerned, they took my money, they took my free movement certificate which I had from the HVO. I did not have that many valuables on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you have -- how much -- did you have a sum of money on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was supposed to buy some material, two cubic metres of stone, so I had 4,000 German marks on me. I also had 300 marks for expenses, so I had a total of 4,300 German marks, maybe some change additionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And they were not given back to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They also took away my car, my -- the things that I had in the car and then later they took my house away and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During your being held in the hangar, were you registered -- were your names written down on some documents? Who did it, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As we were standing against a wall, they ordered us again to take out every single piece of paper from our pockets, everything we had put back, anything from our shoes, from the hair, so that nothing would be found on anyone. I think that they probably were not satisfied enough with what they got, so then the whole situation repeated itself. We took everything out and placed it at our feet. I forgot to say they did not take my watch because one soldier said that this was a Russian watch so it was not good enough quality. However, it was not Russian, it was actually a Swiss watch. Then, again, we placed all our belongings next to our feet, so that process was faster now, it took about 15 minutes. They reviewed all of it and then they said: "Pick up your garbage and put it back in your pockets", so we took all the belongings that were left there and put them in our pockets. Then they ordered us to turn around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garanovic, I would like to know if and to whom you did give your personal data, your name, your family name, and so on, on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They told us to turn around and to walk one by one towards a desk which was placed there, and there was some sawdust there in the corners, so that is where this desk was placed. An HVO soldier sat at this desk. He had a logbook of some kind and then he was entering the data which we gave him, the first and last name, basic data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How did you spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night was nearly fatal for me. It was very cold and I got cramps, very bad cramps in my chest. Given my condition and the cold, the HVO soldiers allowed that several wooden pallets be brought in from outside, so a few wooden pallets were brought in. They are used for loading goods on to trucks. I did not have the strength to bring it by myself, so I remained on concrete. Some people then were sitting on those pallets but most people sat on the concrete. Then they put some kind of a line, which was really an imagined line, they did not draw it, and they said that whoever crossed this line would be shot, so nobody, of course, did it. Nobody wanted to cross it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened the next morning? Were you brought some food, some water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, sometime around 8.30/9.00, they brought some food. There were no toilets. Maybe a few persons were let to go out to relieve themselves. I do not know where these people went to the toilet. In the morning, they brought some food, it was a soup and a slice of bread. We ate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you ask for a doctor at that moment? If so, to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, I really felt fairly bad and I felt I had not much to lose any more, so I told my fellow inmates that I was going to seek medical attention. They said it would be funny to ask for such a thing if it was not sad. However, I said I was going to do it anyway, so I started to look around to see whom I could approach. I singled out one and I did not like the way he looked and then the second one, it was -- there was a second one, so he was somebody who was still in civilian clothes, but he had just joined the police, and so I approached him and said: "Can I ask you something?", he said: "What is it?", I said: "I really need to see a doctor urgently". He asked if I had big problems and I told him I had very big problems. Then immediately another fellow came over and also complained about epilepsy. This civilian man said: "I will come back in about 15 minutes". After about 15 minutes, the civilian -- the -- he wore this sports or track suit, so he came back escorted by a couple of soldiers and he said: "Where are the two men who reported to go and see the doctor?"; the ones around me said: "You are finished". I said "I do not care". So, I reported and the other person did not report. However, this soldier insisted that the second person also step out. I guess he was afraid, so he had not reported. So, then we started -- he went ahead, I followed him and two soldiers were -- one to each side. We came outside to this road. It is really a paved road --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you sign on the photograph you have on the ELMO actually where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: From there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we exited and we went to here, in front of this building. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you circle it with a pen and sign it with the letter "B", please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. Whom were you taken in front of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here in front of this building, so we were brought in front of the entrance to this building and an officer was standing there and two soldiers. There were, I think, maybe more additional two soldiers, I guess they were with him. So the person who brought us to this man who was standing in the middle and he told him: "Commander, these men have health problems and they are seeking medical attention."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you recognise the men to whom the soldier was asking to take care of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised a man, I did not know his name, but I knew him from somewhere. I knew him by sight. Later they said -- at that time I did not know who the commander was around there. I did not even know where I had arrived. This man said -- he first asked the man who was next to me with epilepsy, he asked him: "What is wrong with you? What is your complaint?" This person who was seeking help said: "I am an epileptic" and he mentioned another condition, for which maybe there is no real cure. Then the commander said: "No, you are just pretending. You are pretending that you are sick from what you are complaining about, so you are really acting". He said that he should be immediately taken back to where he was brought from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did this man show to the commander any document concerning his health situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, some documents -- he produced some documents, some papers, I do not know what it was, and the gentleman just looked at his papers and said -- how shall I put this -- that he was just pretending that he was sick, so that he should be taken back. .

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What about you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the commander asked me: "What is wrong with you?" I told him that I had surgery just a couple of months ago. I said that I had undergone surgery in Lubjane, because I did not dare mention the word "Belgrade". He said: "What kind of surgery?" I told him that I got cramps, that I was in pain, that I was very cold, and I showed him the scar from my surgery. He said: "These pains that you feel and the cramps, are due to the cold, because where you spent the night is quite cold." He turned to one of the soldiers and he told him: "What do you think? What about number 12?" He nodded. I did not know what "12" meant, it was around 11.00, what was going to happen at 12, so believe me I was quite afraid. He told me to follow the soldier. I followed the soldier. I entered this building. (Indicating on photograph). That means in here. We went -- we came into the hallway and the hallway went in two directions, left and right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness is signing building B as the one he was accompanied into. Now, let us stop for a moment and go back to the commander. Did you later learn who the commander was and which was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found that out very quickly. I was told when I arrived to cell number 12. In fact, this "12", this was the cell number, that is where I was assigned to go by the commander. When I came into that cell, I immediately learned who this gentleman was. There were two soldiers there who had been punished, I think that they were punished, they were soldiers, they were HVO soldiers. They told me that this was Zlatko Aleksovski, the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You said before that you had had that person before. Can you remember when you had him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion. This was maybe two or three years -- maybe two years prior to that. I remember I went to a restaurant with a friend and this restaurant was on the premises of the correctional centre in Zenica. It was a restaurant were civilians went in the evenings. I went there during the day to meet with this friend who was working at the correctional centre. This friend of mine greeted the gentleman. At that time he told me -- how did he put it -- a corrections officer, that he was a corrections officer in the prison. I must have seen this man a number of times, you know, this was a small town, Zenica, so I never contacted him, but I remembered him as the person from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you describe this man to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a man of about my height, maybe slightly shorter. Maybe slightly receding hair, maybe I would say -- put his height at 165 to 170 metres, so relatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you recognise him if you had an opportunity to see him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given that a lot of time has passed, I am not sure, but if I saw him I think that I could recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you recognise him in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise him. It is the gentleman sitting over there. (Indicating Mr. Aleksovski).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please will it be entered into the record that the witness pointed in the direction of Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Going to the moment in which you met Mr. Aleksovski and the commander of the camp in front of the second hangar, how was he dressed at that moment, when he sent you to the cell number 12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore a camouflage uniform, a hat, a military hat, so he was dressed in military garments with a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You were taken into the building, into a cell within that building; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the cell number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you taken during the time of your staying at Kaonik, did you stay always for the whole time in the same cell or did you change it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the same cell the whole time. I was in there for 31 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, I am introducing in evidence a -- which has already been introduced, a photograph of the building, of the hallway. Can it be shown to the Defence? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I tender in evidence the aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, do you have copies for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: They are not in colour, they are black and white, I am sorry. (Handed). Now, Mr. Garanovic, do you recognise the hallway, the corridor of the building where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you locate cell number 12 for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot see cell number 12 in this picture but it is behind this stove here. That is where cell number 12 is. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Would you please circle it and sign with letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Do you recognise other particular features of that place? For example, the table at the end of the hallway, which was its use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where we received food. In other words, we ate at this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you have other opportunities to leave your cell during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only if we went to the toilet and that was it, there was no other opportunity. Maybe to get water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you locate the entrance to the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hallway. Here is the entrance. (Indicating on photograph). This is where the entrance to the building is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you trace an arrow to locate that part of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: An arrow, just to show where the entrance door was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was there an office in the same building, according to your experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an office at the entrance. To the left there was an office which was the commander's office. To the right was a room which was used for soldiers as relaxation space, that is where they watched television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you please sign with your pen and sign with the letter "B", the commander's office, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph). With the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Yes, with the letter "B". Thank you. Did you have any opportunity from within your cell to see what was happening along the hallway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I suppose the door was locked, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door was locked, but one could hear everything, people talking in the corridor, conversations in the corridor, who was coming or going. Then there was a peephole on the door through which they looked at us. When they were not spying on us, we spied on them. In this way, we had, in a sense, contact with the camp; that is the camp over there, further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you ever taken into Aleksovski's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Would you look at the office and how it was organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could look at the office, not really properly. When you go to the toilet you have to go by quickly. When you are going for water also you have to pass quickly, because there were soldiers in the corridors. They could provoke you and they could beat you up. I saw the office. There was a computer in the office. I saw that. Then there was a secretary, a young lady. There was a table, like any other office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you -- you said you stayed there for 31 days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During this period, were you ever taken out of the cell and out of the camp and by whom and for which reason, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not leave for 31 days. I did not leave my cell, nor did I go outside at all, which means that all that time I was in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you alone in the cell or were there other prisoners with you during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers, the Croats, after four or five days they left and then they brought other prisoners, other inmates to the cell and to the other cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were prisoners taken away for forced labour, for trench digging, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was done on a daily basis. Almost everyone was taken to do forced labour. There was no possibility of questioning it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How was this organised? Who did actually call out the prisoners who had to be taken trench digging daily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you. The system of taking people, taking prisoners to dig trenches, was as follows: in the morning or in the afternoon or in the evening, a soldier, a policeman called Ljubo, would call out the names of people. He had a piece of paper on him and he read out the names of the people who had to go to dig on the front-lines. However, not only that, but sometimes the list was extended by the door being opened and them picking out people and taking them to the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where did Ljubo take the list from? Who did give Ljubo the list of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see. The office was there, from where the whole system was managed. I personally saw once Ljubo entering, passing along the corridor, taking a piece of paper. What was on that paper, I do not know. I was going to get water and Ljubo was calling out the names. That was the time when, in order to save myself from going to the front-line and to avoid the possibility of me being picked out when he opened the door, this was the way for me to save myself, by not being in the cell. But if he called out my name, then there was no escape, regardless of the fact that I was outside in the corridor. So that we roughly envisaged when Ljubo would come. Then we knocked on the door. Ljubo was rather loud, because we could hear him entering from the outside even. So we would knock on the door to ask to fetch water or to go to the toilet. Then the guard would open the door. I would go out. I can say that I did that very often, while, in the meantime, Ljubo would go in, call out the names, or simply open the door and hand-pick people for digging trenches and working on the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us go back to the list. Where did Ljubo take that list from when you saw him entering the office, Aleksovski's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He entered the office. There is no question about it. I said I just saw him once from a kind of a window with a glass in it, taking this list through the window. Whether this was the list of names, I could not read it, but he would say the names of the people who had to come out. He would call out those names every morning. I would be going from this direction towards the toilet, (indicating on photograph) to get water and Ljubo would come in and go in that direction. He would go along the corridor and call out the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I have another question: how did you succeed in never being called off for work? That work, I suppose, was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I was in such a condition that I took advantage of every possibility to avoid being taken there. Because I was not afraid for myself, but I was afraid that when Ljubo handed me over, up there on the front-line, because of my condition, I would not be able to work and there was a possibility of them executing me over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did some of the prisoners who were taken trench digging not come back, and for which reason? How did they explain that to you? Was that explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my cell, one man was killed. He was killed on the front-lines. His name was -- should I give you his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Omer Lugonic. He was from Teslic. The Serbs forced him to go to Tesanj. He was captured on the road and he was killed while digging on the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: This did you learn from other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And Ljubo came to collect some of his things, if anything was left. When Ljubo came back -- because Ljubo probably did not go to the front-lines, he probably handed over these prisoners to someone else. He would hand them over at the front to other soldiers and that was where the danger was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You spent most of the time in your cell, night and day. Did you ever see or hear or remember seeing or hearing something unusual during your stay at Kaonik; beatings, screams, sounds, speeches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very frequently, or relatively frequently. I did hear beatings rather far away in the other cells. Some people were tortured then in the corridor. We just listened when this was happening, when they were beaten up. But from my cell, two guys were taken out and beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mustafa Hodzic and Almir Hodzic, Almir Hodzic. That has been imprinted in my memory because they beat them so fiercely that Almir had a serious spine injury. He is still alive, but he is suffering from the consequences of this spine injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about what has happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, after such cries, we did not talk. We were quiet for hours. When a man comes in, he does not talk. He has suffered terrible torture and fear. We hardly talked at all straight away, but afterwards then he would say that somebody had beat him using karate blows or judo hits and among other things this young man told me that even Zlatko had hit him once or twice as he passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What about you, were you personally beaten and mistreated, and by whom, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was mistreated every single moment. We were all mistreated. For instance, you see, a man comes in at 3.00 am. He wakes you up like a ghost demanding gold, "give me your gold", what do you do then? All this was mistreatment. I personally was not physically abused. I was not beaten, I was not beaten. I was not hurt by beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You told us the commander's office was near to your cell. Who usually worked with Aleksovski? You mentioned a woman, was she a part of the staff or was she a prisoner, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she was a woman employed there. She was the secretary in that office. She probably used the computer as well. Perhaps Zlatko did not know how to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was there a Dzemo who did help Aleksovski as well in his job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among others, there was this Dzemo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What was he supposed to do in that context? Which was his role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what his role was, but I do know that he mistreated people, that he provoked them, that he sang some songs which we did not like. You know, he kept the situation tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Which kind of songs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The songs -- the Croats do not have many songs. They have: "Here is the dawn, here is the day", we have Dzure and Boban, they just have two many songs, they just have folk songs that they know how to sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you remember listening to speeches or other hymns being played or being given, delivered in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not listen to any hymns, but, you see, late at night when everything is quiet, they would sometimes send out very loud sounds or signals which would wake us up. These signals are unknown to me, was probably some kind of a loud speaker which produced this sound. All this was intended to intimidate us, to frighten us, to exhaust us, so as to prevent us from having a quiet sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you registered by the Red Cross, and when, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was on 24th April that the Red Cross registered us. I think it was 24th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: When were you released and in which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were civilians, and it was under those conditions that we were released. Those of us who registered as civilians. However, the HVO soldiers were sitting there, Dzemo among them, in the evening, and they were talking, that in Zenica they only wanted soldiers for an exchange and not civilians, so who registered as a soldier, he would be exchanged and who did not, he would be lost. Some fell for this and so they stayed longer in this camp. They were probably afterwards exchanged even though they were not soldiers but were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I have no more questions, your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Garanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I should like to ask the technicians to put on the screen the document which is on the ELMO, please. Can we see it on the screen? Thank you. I think we have to make it clear that the letter "A", the one next to the letter "B", is worth nothing, to avoid any confusion. I think this should be done, do you not think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, which exhibit number is it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I think there is no point in asking Mr. Mikulicic whether he wishes to begin the cross-examination now. We thank the Prosecutor for being so punctual, so we shall now have our lunch break and have a good lunch everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: After a week of work, we are well into half of this week, and I think that perhaps all of us are quite tired, but also satisfied with the work we have done. I think that these are two parameters of high quality work, but, at the end, we will be judged too. So we are going to resume our sitting and I think that we have to have the witness brought in, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. This morning you answered questions from the Prosecution. Now, you are going to answer questions put to you by the Defence counsel of Mr. Aleksovski. Therefore, Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The cross-examination of Mr. Garanovic will be conducted by my learned colleague, Mr. Joka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it please the court, I am Mr. Joka, one of the counsel for the accused. I would like to ask you some questions and I would like you to respond to them shortly and succinctly. First, I would like to correct -- I would like you to correct me if I misunderstood any of your statement given during your testimony. Is it true that in Stojkovici, when you were arrested, it was the HVO police who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Is it true that you were also searched there by the HVO police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we were boarding the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you were escorted to the Kaonik facility by the HVO police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the HVO police took away your personal belongings there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
