utterances.text: Is it correct that the person in charge in the hangar -- that is the HVO police was also in charge of the hangar where you were first brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that the HVO police was in charge of it. It was not just a hangar, it was a camp and the person in charge there, by the logic of things, was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Let us leave alone the logic of things -- no, I am talking about the first night when you were told to put your hands against a wall and things like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the HVO police who did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Is it also true that the HVO police also registered you when you first arrived in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were the HVO police and the HVO military there, so they were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: In other words, we are talking about the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well, now that we have determined that, I would like to take you to the place where you described how this compound looked. You talked about the bend and the building around the bend to the right. You also mentioned the HVO in that connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You probably refer to the barracks building, when you turn towards Busovaca. There to the right, on the right-hand side, there was a barracks where the HVO soldiers were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: That is correct. Could we please see the photograph which was offered into evidence by the Prosecution, where the witness marked the buildings under "A" and "B"? If we could use that picture for the witness to also identify these barracks. Thank you. (Handed). If you could, please show us on this photograph this building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph). The barracks is on the road from Kaonik to Busovaca and there is a right turn off and this is the barracks here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Could you, please, mark it and put the next letter in the alphabet -- that is the letter "C" -- next to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You can also mark it with the letter "C". Thank you. Could you tell us, do you know which units were in these barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Thank you, I am finished as far as the photograph is concerned. I would like to move on to the next area. Except for the HVO units, regardless of whether it was the military or police, did you see any guards around this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my stay, I was unable to see anyone there because it was around the bend and I never left to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well. Where you were staying, did you see any guards there, in the building where this cell number 12 was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards were always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Now, were these the guards or the HVO troops, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the soldiers who were assigned to control this area, to guard posts, to guard duties there. Those were the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: So these were the HVO soldiers exclusively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were no prison guards. Not in the civilian sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well. You constantly use one term, you use the term "commander". Do you distinguish between "commander" and "warden" or "director"; is there a difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Could you please describe it to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he is a director he is like director of, let us say, a school. If he is a commander, he is a commander of some kind of military unit or military organisation. A director can be -- if you will, in this case, something like a civilian prison, as in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You explained how you understand it. You told the Trial Chamber how you knew of the commander, that you saw him in the garden of the correctional centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not in the gardens. I saw him in passing in the hallway on the way to this garden.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Did you go to that garden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is a very nice restaurant the there, so a lot of people went there to have coffee and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Now, who all went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know that the employees of the correctional centre, the police and the members of the secret police, can have access to this garden by showing their ID cards; in other words, it was not open to the public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not true. This was a public premise which was owned by the correctional centre and you, too, could go in there when you came to Zenica to have a cup of tea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Let us go back to Zlatko Aleksovski. You said that when you first saw him that he was wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Of course, in the camp. Did he have any insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not remember that. I really do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zlatko Aleksovski had any kind of a conflict with any of the soldiers or guards regarding their visiting the prisoners, given that they were armed? Are you familiar with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that Zlatko disproved -- disagreed with some actions of these soldiers, because any HVO soldier had a right to come there and say: "You know, somebody of my own was killed", then he could enter those cells and go and beat up on anyone. I think that there were times when Zlatko did not agree with such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: When you said that you were not feeling well and you asked to be taken to the director to complain to him, he was not a director. When you went to Zlatko Aleksovski and when you complained about your surgery and the effects of it, was there discussion about getting a physician then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I needed a doctor. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said: "Sir, commander, I need to see a physician. I have terrible pains, I have cramps in my chest." He told me: "What was the surgery about?" Then I showed him the scar. He said: "You cannot get assistance here for your condition. There is not such a doctor here who can help you with this, so nobody here can give you the right assistance". Then he turned to the soldier and he also told me: "You have this cramps and these pains because of the cold".

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, you already mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he told everything else that I related.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: And this is how you ended up in cell number 12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were you able to sleep there, and if you were, where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some boards -- in fact, there was more like these pallets and there was some kind of a fabric on top of these boards and one blanket, just a single blanket. That is where I slept, on those boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: So was that like an improvised bed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an improvised bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Was that a little better, better or significantly better than the conditions that you had previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These presented better conditions because I do not think that I would have survived. I think that I would have committed suicide in the other there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You said that there were also two Croats there, two soldiers, two HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Did they have different conditions from you in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our conditions did not intersect there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: So you had, what, the same treatment? Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a prisoner. I was outside of the law. I think that they were protected by law. I was not protected by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: No, no, no. My question was about the living conditions. Did you have -- did they have beds --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, we had the same conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You mean food and everything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the conditions were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You told us about the little window through which you observed them a little bit and they observed you a little bit. Did you see through that little opening the guards in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards were always there, around near the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: So there was not a moment when there were no guards in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw that there were no guards in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well, let us go back to your cell. Were the doors to your cell locked -- I mean closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: In such a way that they could not be opened by anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door could not be opened from inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Did you know how they were closed from the outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was like a metal bar or a metal handle that would be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Was it like a sliding bar or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: So there was no lock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no lock.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Was there a key?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no key.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know where people who remained in the hangar received their food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While they were in the hangar, they received their food in the hangar and when they went to dig at the front-lines, I think that that is where I suppose they were getting their food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: So that is an assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: In the future, I would just like you to stay within the realm of what you know positively and about what you just conjecture, please just say that you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you asked me, so I answered the way you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well. We are moving now to the forced labour issue. You talked about Ljubo, the policeman, who called people out and who selected them. Do you know unequivocally who put together these lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who compiled these lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it was done in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: No, my question was just who made them, not where they were made. You also mentioned the tragic fate of Omer Lugonic; he was killed at the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know that unequivocally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Is it something that others told you or you have first-hand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew quite a bit there, --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Please, just answer. Was it something that you heard about or something that you actually observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, Omer was taken -- Ljubo had selected me to go to the front-lines. However, a soldier engaged Ljubo in a conversation for a little while and I knew that I was unable to work, it would have been too hard for me, so I used those several moments that I had while this soldier was talking to Ljubo --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Garanovic, you already told us this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I did not say this: I pulled back, by two metres about -- when Ljubo came back, I was not in the same place where I was when Ljubo first called me out. Then he turned around and he saw a man reading a book and this was Omer Lugonic. He was probably annoyed by that. He said: "You who are reading this book, you are coming with us". Then Omer told me that it was terrible on the front-lines, that the snipers were shooting there --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: No, I am just trying to ask you whether you know how he was killed, the circumstances in which he was killed, not how he left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ljubo came back and he asked for Ljubo's belongings. The word came that he was killed by the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You are saying that you know about his death from what other people said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You also said that at night you could hear screams, something that would be related to mistreatment or torture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was all part of the intimidation, part of driving people crazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were these screams from cells or from some audio tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Just if you know this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had -- how can I call it -- they had loud speakers, so they would play some tapes very loud when it was very quiet, when it was silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: And you could distinguish between when this was played back and when it was alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, these were horrible sounds. These were like dying sounds --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, but the first, second, third times, was it always the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Once I could make out sounds like "cut his throat", "slit his throat". I do not know whether it was the guard saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: So you do not know whether this was going on for real or if this was a play-back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was a play-back and it was done in order to intimidate us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know whether the guards, including this Ljubo, was at one point mobilised to go to the front-lines; do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they did go to the front-lines. Directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went there often. Among them, at the front-line, Anto Cakic was wounded. I know that he was wounded at the front-line and I heard of others, both from the men in the cells that they were taken to the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, that would also mean that some of the guards were wounded too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the front-lines of the guards?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were any of the guards wounded in the Kaonik itself, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. There was a shell -- a shell was lobbed near the barracks and two of the guards were slightly wounded. One I think had a head injury. I think the other had a leg injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I only have a couple more questions for you. You mentioned a certain Dzemo. Do you know what his status was at Kaonik? Was he an HVO member; was he a guard; a prisoner or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a bad guy who was their runner. He probably had something in Zenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: I am not asking whether he was a positive or negative character. Do you know what his status was at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what his status was. I know that he was constantly provoking, intimidating, mistreating the inmates and he was driving us all crazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know what his ethnic background is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know what his religion is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is nothing, but I think that he would be of -- that his religion would be Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Tribunal, do you still have a stone-cutting company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Did you sell the one that you used to have before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I sold it, but at a much lower price.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: What year did you sell it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: What year did you sell it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: To whom did you sell it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the person who was there, to Ratko Strukar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Is that the same young man you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were you an eye-witness or in a way present when the first conflicts occurred in Travnik in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In October?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, when the first conflicts broke out between the HVO and the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not travel to Travnik very often. I usually went to Zenica. I did not belong to the BiH army or any other military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Did you ever wear a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Of not a single military formation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Will you please tell us, after having told us how, for almost a month, you managed to avoid going for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I managed to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, did that have anything to do with your health?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used that too, in a sense, as an excuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Let me ask you for your assessment. Did you manage not to engage in forced labour for a month because you were skilful or because you were so sick?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Objection. This questioning requires a judgement. I am sorry, your Honours, I have to object to this sort of question which implies a judgement on the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, I think that we should avoid any judgement on the testimony and the witness, so you can put the question but without any judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I shall rephrase the question. Did you go to cell number 12 because of your physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: One further question only, does the name Rozika Kordic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that people were saying that she was a doctor, but I really do not know. No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You do not know that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you too. Any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I have some additional questions related to the cross-examination we have heard now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Garanovic, I know you already answered that, but I would like you to state again, after having been cross-examined, from whose office was the sheet of paper taken by Ljubo before he went to the cell to call off the names of those who had to go trench digging. Whose office was that, can you say it again to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the office of the commander, Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. Second question: you told the court about sounds that were heard and, according to you, intentionally transmitted during the night in order to intimidate and disturb the prisoners. Particularly, you said you had an opportunity to hear the sounds of somebody being slaughtered and voices saying: "Slaughter him, slaughter him". Again, can you say whether this was real or recorded -- whether all was recorded -- were these noises relating to something that was really happening that moment or whether they were registered and just transmitted for the same reasons you had mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this was broadcast at that moment, but that the soldier who was in the corridor was saying: "Slaughter him, slaughter him". This was to frighten the inmates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for the interruption, but I think you want to say something. You have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, your Honour. I have an objection of the same nature. This time the witness is being asked something that we were overruled to ask; that is, his assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is necessary to put a precise question regarding the facts rather than the opinions. I think that this applies to both the Defence and the Prosecution. Therefore, I think it is not a good idea to ask: "what is your opinion", but: "what do you know about" this or that. Would you please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I agree and I will fully comply with what you say. Let me only underline that one thing is to ask a witness about an opinion about facts and the other thing is asking a witness about something that affects his morality and his moral attitude towards what he is experiencing. Anyway, I will fully comply. I do understand and I share what you suggested. My question can be restated in this way: were these sounds, these voices, and these phrases, transmitted through a microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through a loud speaker, a large, loud speaker, through a sound system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And could he hear other voices during his stay there in the night saying phrases different from: "I will slaughter him, slaughter him"? Did he have an opportunity to hear other voices saying something very precise as to Muslims, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was listening to a voice, a voice very similar to Kordic's voice, very similar. That was at the very beginning. I think this was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. This goes beyond the cross-examination, the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The question goes beyond the scope of the cross-examination, Mr. Prosecutor. So, please withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. I will withdraw the question. Thank you, Mr. President. Another question relates to cross-examination and it is concerning the cell where the witness was taken after having shown his scar and explained his physical situation to Aleksovski. The question is this: were those taken to that cell, all of them in bad physical conditions, did they have any problems with health? First question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Most of them did not have any health problems, aside from the mental condition, though there were people who were sick. There was a man who needed haemodialysis, he was not in my cell but in another cell. That was the situation, so that there were some people who were ill, but they were not given medical attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: People from your cell, was it people in your cell, were they taken to trench digging as well as people from other cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly -- most of them, more or less all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. No other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Garanovic, the noise you referred to that was reminiscent of a loud speaker or a tape being played, did it always come from the same direction and from the same spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the same direction and from the same spot. It was there somewhere within that hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, the direction from which it came did not change, or did it change sometimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not change, it did not change. It always came from the same direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. You have completed your testimony. We thank you very much for having come and a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, I think you are getting ready for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the next witness is brought into the court, I am compelled to make an application on behalf of the witness. The witness, your Honours, is witness number 6 on the inventory of witnesses filed, dated 23rd February. On his behalf, your Honours, I am seeking protective measures; I am seeking, your Honours, that the witness be assigned a pseudonym and also that the image of his face be distorted during the course of his testimony. We have indicated that we would be applying for these protective measures to Mr. Mikulicic and I understand -- I believe that learned Defence counsel has no objection to my application and, therefore, I submit that your Honours be pleased to grant the protective measures I am seeking in respect of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar and the usher, will you wait for a moment, we still have not decided. I want to ask you, Mr. Mikulicic, whether you have any objection or not to this application?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Registrar and the usher, you may continue to take the necessary steps, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It is the president who is speaking to you. You are going to read the statement that the Registrar is going to give to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated. You can put your headphones on like this, on top of your head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is better now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you for coming here to appear before the International Criminal Tribunal. You are going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor, Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. WITNESS I

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, before you testify, I would ask you to look at the sheet of paper and confirm whether the name which appears on this is your name or not. May this be shown to the witness, your Honours? Thereafter it may be shown to learned counsel for the accused. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit under seal, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, in the course of these proceedings, you will be referred to as "Witness I". Witness, could you please state to this court what your ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak, of Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What is your age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I am taking you to the events of April of 1993. Do you remember the 14th day of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember what you did on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th in the morning at 6.00, six of us, six trucks went towards Metkovici for goods, trucks with trailers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you able to reach Metkovici that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How far were you able to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thirty kilometres from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where would that be, 30 kilometres from Zenica, where would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were stopped just outside Novi Travnik, locality called Stojkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who stopped you in Stojkovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were stopped at Stojkovici by the army of the HVO, the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know it was the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in camouflage uniforms and wore HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember, about how many soldiers were there at the point you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were four to five soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: At about what time was it in the morning when you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was exactly 6.50 am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you were stopped by the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were stopped, we were ordered to park the trucks on the left-hand side of the carriageway. There were large meadows there and we parked the trucks. We got out and, under escort of those soldiers, we were taken up to a place called Kace. These were sheds of the former army. There was a compound with a big gate to it and we were taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were all of you taken to this compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of us were taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you were taken to that compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there, we were shut up in a container and there were some civilian prisoners there already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many civilian prisoners were there in the container at the time you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The container consisted of two parts: one part was narrower and the other was wider. In the wider part, one could hear voices of people who were imprisoned there and when we were brought there, there was about seven of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In which part of the container were you detained? Was it in the wider part or the narrower part of the container?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were put in the narrower part of the container and there were 13 or 14 of us in that narrower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate size of this part of the container that you were put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the width could not have been more than one metre 30 and in lengths perhaps it was 180, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. How long were you locked up in this part of the container?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent the whole day there, so that in the evening one really could not stand it any more because the only way one could stay there was standing straight up, upright. Then in the evening I and another one of the prisoners, who was director of the mines in Zenica, went into a bus and we spent the night there, so that we left the container about eight o'clock in the evening. That was the first time we left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you left the container, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went to the bus to spend the night, in the morning the drivers came for us and we were ordered to drive the trucks into the compound where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after the buses were driven into the compound where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after the buses were driven into the compound where you earlier were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Transport -- city transport bus was brought there that evening, probably to provide more space for those people in the container, so that they could sit there instead of standing upright, as I said. So we spent the night in that bus. Then in the morning, we were told to fetch our trucks and drive them into the compound of the barracks, which was the barracks of the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About how many people were taken to the barracks of the former Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was at least 50 of us in that container, at least 50 there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know where these barracks were situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to the sheds of the Kaonik prison, but I am talking about the container where we were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, so from the container, were you taken elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening the bus came, after midnight this must have been. We were loaded on to the bus and from there we were taken to Kaonik, to the former barracks, also a military barracks. They took us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Those were the barracks in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who brought you to the barracks in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, you know who; the HVO army. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was the bus in which you were transported to Kaonik escorted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who escorted the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a car in front with HVO soldiers inside and behind us there was another car with HVO soldiers also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About what time of the night did you reach Kaonik barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened upon reaching the Kaonik barracks, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bus stopped just in front of the shed and we were told to get out and enter. Inside there were at least 150 people held prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened when you entered this building in the Kaonik barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as we got there, we were told to line up against the wall; to raise our hands up for them to search us to see whether we had any weapons or knives, and that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you searched as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And after the search, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we were all searched, we were pulled aside, we were told to move to the side and that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were your personal details taken down at the barracks thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who took down your personal details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was just a regular person in uniform, I guess. He was a soldier and he was sitting at a desk and taking down our data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you see any others in HVO uniform at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As he was taking our data, there were two men in front of the door and when we got there, there were at least seven or eight there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I seek permission to show the witness an aerial photograph of the camp, which is already admitted into evidence, your Honours? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 58; right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, would you please look at the exhibit on the ELMO and point out the place where you were ordered to get off the bus when you were brought to Kaonik that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How shall I show it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You may use one of the highlighters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I would ask you to circle the building to which you went in first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where we were brought. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please circle that and please place the letter "A" beside that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So it was to that building that you were first brought upon reaching Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it was in that building that you were searched -- you, together with the others -- and registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, witness, could you tell this court, you were brought in the night; what happened the following morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as we arrived there, and after we were registered and our belongings were taken away from us, they immediately took us -- not all of us but about 20 or 30 of us, we were placed in a vehicle and we were taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many of you were taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my group, it was one truckload, that was 25 to 30 persons. This was a village called Jelinak and that is where I went to dig throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long did you have to dig trenches upon being taken to Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We always went digging early in the morning, pre-dawn, and until it was dark, so that means if we left early in the morning, we would come back after dark. If we went early in the morning, that would be before the dawn, we would just dig all day long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On how many occasions were you taken to Jelinak for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken there almost daily, until the moment when I was wounded on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On all those occasions, were a group of prisoners taken together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were simply coming and selecting people who they wanted to -- first they would go for -- ask for volunteers. If there were none, they would say: "You, you, you, you and you". We would have to go and dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would select the prisoners in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would simply come in, he would approach us as we were sitting on those pallets and he would say: "you, you and you". He would select a group and we had to follow him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who is it that would say: "You, you and you", approaching the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, this would be a soldier, their soldier, an HVO soldier in a camouflage uniform, and he would select us and take us to dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that you were taken daily until the day you got wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you describe to this court the incident in which you got wounded when you were taken trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the night between 20th and 21st, we went digging with that group and it was four of us, at this location we were supposed to dig. Two of them were separated out from us, or put us about 20 metres apart. This was on the edge of the village of Jelinak. They told us to dig a trench about two by three metres and we spent digging it almost the entire night, until we started hearing shells, the shelling was starting. So, at that moment, we started running. We came into the village of Jelinak and I guess their command post was there -- you know, some kind of panic ensued. An HVO soldier came up and he said: "Just line them up against a wall. We have nothing else to do with them, let us shoot them". Then an old man said: "Please do not, for Christ's sake, do not." He swore at Christ but then he changed his mind. He said: "turn around". We did. He told us to sit down and we did. He told us to sit down. Then another soldier came and gave us a pack of Corona cigarettes: "I know that you drivers like to smoke Marlboro, but we do not have it, so Corona will do". We each took a cigarette, lit it up, asked for some water because we were not receiving water over there. That is there was some water where we were digging, but there were, among the soldiers, those who allowed us to drink water, but certain soldiers in this -- I noticed one in a camouflage uniform and I noticed that they were afraid of him. So, when we would ask of him to drink water, he would never give us, but when he would move away, 15 or 20 metres, they told us: "Go on now, drink". At that time when they did not shoot us, they took us down towards Loncari and back towards the camp and there was a vehicle coming, Praga coming from the direction of Loncari with this fragmentation bullets. At that time they said: "lie down, because it is dangerous". At that point I was hit and wounded in my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were wounded on your hand, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On which hand were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you were wounded on the right hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was wounded, the HVO soldier took a bandage and bandaged my hand. When we reached the barracks, we were taken to where the cells were. I later heard that these were the solitaries and I spent about three or four hours there with another wounded person who was also wounded as I was, but over on the other side. When it dawned -- when the morning came around 8.00 or 9.00 o'clock, I was taken to the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were brought back and you were taken to the cells. Now, could you -- would you be able to identify the building in which the cells were, looking at the photograph that is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you please look at the photograph, witness, and, using the pointer, could you please point out the building to which you were taken after being wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, please. Go ahead. Using a highlighter marker pen could you please circle the second building to which you were taken to after being wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. It is this one. (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please mark that building with the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In the cell that you were put into, were there others detained in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was only the other person who was wounded and myself, and the cell in which we were put was the solitary cell and that is where I was and the person who was wounded in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who was wounded in the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not, but I know that he is somewhere from the Tesanj area. I used to know his name, but I cannot recall it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances under which he was wounded in the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was always during the digging and while they were withdrawing, he was hit with a shell fragment and wounded in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: May I have your Honour's permission to show the witness an extract from P4? These have been exhibited before. There are copies for your Honours and my learned friend. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please place that on the ELMO, usher? Witness I, could you please look at the map that is on the ELMO. Carefully look at that map. Could you, please, point out the place, the village Jelinak where you said you were taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please circle that area and mark it with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: It was whilst trench digging in that area that you got wounded in your right hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as we were withdrawing. I was wounded in the village of Loncari, as we were already going back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Witness, you said you were brought back to the camp and put into a cell; what happened after you were put into that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the time came, that is when the HVO soldier came to get me and the other person who was there with me. He took us in a vehicle to Busovaca, to this health centre. I was put in a cast, on my open wound, and I was told to go back into the vehicle, that I was not allowed to walk around. I had to wait for this colleague of mine. They could not find the shrapnel in his back, so they did not do anything to him. When we came back I was placed in cell number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, is there a chance of you finishing the examination-in-chief by four o'clock?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I may go a little beyond four o'clock. Maybe five or 10 minutes beyond four o'clock, not more than that, if your Honours would permit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. I think that it would be a good idea to have a break for the benefit of the interpreters and ourselves as well. We will resume work at 4.10 pm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, would you like to take over -- no, no, I am sorry. I beg your pardon, we had not finished with the examination in chief. Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I will not take very long, your Honours. Witness I, before the recess, in answer to my question, you said to this court that from the health centre you were brought back and put into cell number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You were put into cell number 5; were there others in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were two soldiers of the BiH army imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember the condition of those two soldiers who were in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. They were beaten up more or less, beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to speak to the two soldiers in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not want to talk. They did not trust me, they did not know who I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where did you observe injuries, or where were they beaten, on which part of their bodies were they beaten, from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their back, their face, their arms, their whole body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So, for how long were you in that cell, witness, in cell number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember anything in particular happening to you whilst you were in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came from the health centre my hand was in a cast and the next day, or maybe even the day after, the door opened and a soldier in uniform entered. He just looked at me and he hit me real hard, so that I had a bruise, black eye, for almost two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who was the soldier who hit your eye?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was their soldier but I do not know his name. They asked me if I could recognise him, but I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who asked you if you could recognise the soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One morning a guard came, the guard of the cells and he told me that the commander needed me, so I went -- he was taken -- I was taken to the place where the gentleman was sitting and he asked me whether I had hit myself while digging with a shovel or with a pickaxe. "No", I said, "I was hit in the cell".

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know that the person who questioned you was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guard who came for me, he said that we had to go -- I had to go and see the commander, he wanted to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did the commander introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As soon as I entered the office, I know where it was I entered, and the man who brought me said: "There you are. You have to go and see so and so".

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In relation to your cell, to cell number 5, where was the commander's office? Was it in the same building or was it in a different building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same building. In the same building, off the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So, how did you respond to the commander's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me whether I had hit myself with a shovel or a pickaxe while digging and I said: "No", that I had not hit myself, but that I had been hit by one of the HVO soldiers who simply entered the cell and hit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did the commander ask you any further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, witness, would you be able to describe the physical appearance of the commander whom you saw in that office that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please, to this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man who received me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, the man who received you in the commander's office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There he is over there, sitting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, has it entered the record that the witness has pointed in the direction of Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I do not think you clarified how the witness was hit by the soldier who entered the cell, was it by his fist --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour, I will go back to that issue. Now, witness, I will take you back to the incident where you were hit by a soldier. Would you tell this court -- now, you said you were in cell number 5 that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I came from the health centre and they took me to cell number 5. The next day, or the day after, the door opened. This HVO soldier entered. We were sitting down on these planks nailed together, and he simply entered and hit me with his left hand against my right eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Witness, when you were in the commander's office, you said to the commander -- that is the accused, to whom you pointed out a while ago -- that you were hit by a soldier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, do you know whether any action was taken against the soldier who hit you in the cell, inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, after that conversation with the commander, were you brought back to the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you brought back to the same cell that you were in earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened to you thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the cell until I was released home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, do you know when you were released from custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was released on the 26th or the 27th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances under which you were released from custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of my colleagues, who is also a driver, he was wounded on the 22nd, and seriously wounded, so that he was transferred from Busovaca to Zenica to the hospital there and when the report came that he was in the hospital in Zenica, people started asking where we were, because nobody knew where we were, and when he told them that we were at Kaonik, the Red Cross came and the next day, or the day after, they released us, the six of us were released. But this driver who had been wounded, he was already in Zenica by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, do you know how this colleague of yours -- do you know how he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also wounded in his right arm, but it was a very serious wound, so that his arm was in special wires for five months. It was a very serious injury and that is why he was transferred to Zenica in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, I am taking you back to the hangar building that you were originally detained in. Do you remember the conditions in that building, the building which you marked with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a hangar which is about 35 metres long and wide, between 18 and 20 metres, which has absolutely no partitions, just supporting concrete pillars. The floor was concrete too, but there was quite a bit of earth over the concrete and we had nothing to sit on. We would go out to fetch these pallets. These are things used for transportation of goods, when loading on to trucks, and we would sit or lie on these pallets. There was no toilet. The toilet was outside the building, across the path. It was made there. It was made by us prisoners as a latrine. There was no water. There was a barrel and a pail and that is how we drank water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have heating inside the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we had no heating. At the end of the building was this barrel with holes in it and sometimes we could make a fire in it. One cannot certainly describe it as having been comfortable and warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, what about the conditions in the cell in which you were detained, the building which you marked with the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this cell, the conditions were far better because when we were in that upper building there were a lot of people imprisoned there. When food was brought, there was a table of about two metres in length, and we would be given a fixed amount of time to eat. For instance, they would say: "In 20 minutes you have to finish your meal". Can you imagine, 200 men, when they rush to the table. I was in that building for maybe four or five days and all that I managed to get would be a piece of bread, as a meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What facilities did you have for sleeping in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were just boards, nailed together, from one wall to the other. They were about 40 or 50 metres above floor level. They were like wooden boxes, and that is what we slept on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you said you were released from detention on 26th or 27th April 1993; and where were you taken to upon your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honours. Before I wind up, I would like documents Exhibit 58 and 59, I would move that those documents be admitted into evidence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Meddegoda, I did not understand your question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I marked two documents, your Honours, P58 and 59. I move that those documents be admitted into evidence, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, we seem to have developed a habit to start with you, so you have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence counsel is grateful, but colleague Joka will be cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it please the court. First I would like that the witness be shown the exhibit number 58, the photograph of the Kaonik camp. I would like to start my questioning by showing this photograph first. (Handed). May we now -- in this photograph, you identified two buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You marked them with letters A and B and, as you can see, there are additional buildings here. Can you identify any additional buildings here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You have a building by the road and you have several buildings behind the buildings A and B. You cannot identify a single one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no further use for the exhibit number 58. You stated to the Trial Chamber that it was six drivers who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Among them was a driver named Cajdric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Did he have money on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all had money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interrupt my learned friend, may I submit to your Honours that because the witness has protective measures that the court be pleased to move into private session with the names of the other colleagues being divulged in cross-examination, which would mean, in turn, that the witness's own identity might get revealed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I was aware of that. If we need to cite names, we better have a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we can reach our desired statements without going into the private session. I think that I can ask my questions in such a way as not to reveal ... I am saying this for simplicity's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. If we respect the requirement to protect the witness, we can continue in public session, can we not, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour, we could continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, you may continue, Mr. Joka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: I thank you for your drawing attention to the matter, and I will try to present in a manner where no names are mentioned. Was there a colleague among the ones who were arrested with the money who gave his money to the safe-keeping of a Croat soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, we were over 200 in this hangar. I know what you are trying to ask me. 150 people were robbed, 150 people. They even took their clothes and footwear. I know what you are trying to ask me, sir. Let me tell you, when they placed me against a wall and started searching me, this man, Cajdric, he was a colleague of mine --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Just please do not mention his name. If I do not, please you do not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, yes. I do not know who this person was, whether he was a policeman or a soldier, but I know him. He asked him: "what are you doing here?" He said: "I was going to get some merchandise". It is true that this man said: "I have some extra money on me". He gave him the money and it is true that this money was then returned, but do not forget 150 people were robbed completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Could you tell us what amount that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean how much money the driver gave to this man of yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: It was not my man, it was just a man.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 10 to 12,000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on. When you described the situation when you were digging trenches, you said to the Trial Chamber that the HVO soldiers behaved in a different manner, for instance, some allowed you to drink water. But when there was a particular man present there, it seemed as if they, themselves, were afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I do not know who it was. I do not know this man, he was not a local.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Was there anything special about this man that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was nothing like that. When we went digging, there were two or three guards who guarded us. It was -- most of it was done during the night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You said during the night of the 20th to 21st there was a shelling and everybody fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Right. Did anybody stop you, you who were digging, were you prevented from fleeing in that initial phase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody stopped us because they were fleeing themselves. We just collected the shovels and ran.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You said that after you were wounded you were placed in a cell and that two men who were there were BiH army soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: How do you know they were BiH army soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could not have had an HVO soldier in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Is that an assumption of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not an assumption, it is certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: But did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were told -- they told me this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: But you said that nobody wanted to talk to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first nobody talked to me, but later when I was told that I would go, I even -- I even got some phone numbers to call people to tell them were certain people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were these two people in civilian clothes or in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed, sort of, sloppily.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what "sloppily" means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has trousers -- shoes without laces, some kind of trousers and camouflage -- and a jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: You know that a soldier and a civilian can be dressed sloppily. Can you explain what it was -- what it meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that it can happen to both the civilian and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: I do not know what "sloppy" means. In your sense of the word, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is unmatched, it can be camouflage top or camouflage trousers and torn sweater or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were there any insignia of rank there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: After you were wounded, were you, again, taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: I would like to move on to the episode with the director or warden. Did the director ask you explicitly whether you could recognise the HVO soldier who hit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, he was not my director and I did not know him. Only the turnkey came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: I know that. What did the man ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me: "Did you hit yourself while you were digging trenches with a shovel or a pickaxe?". I said: "No. No, I was not hit with either a shovel or a pickaxe, but I received a blow from a soldier who opened the door, who entered and he hit me with his right arm" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: But did the director ask you whether you could identify this soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told him that I could not identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: So he did ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Did the director ask you other things or was the discussion just regarding your injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Let us not deal in probabilities. Did he ask anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not ask me anything else. He said: "can you recognise the man who hit you?". I said I could not, even though I could have recognised him, but for my own safety, I told him that I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Now, for my own sake, I am not sure whether I had understood this correctly, when you talked about your colleague who received the severe injury in his arm, did you say that he was transferred to the health centre at Busovaca and from there to the Zenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where he was transferred, whether it was to the health centre in Busovaca or to the Zenica hospital, but once he was in the hospital, and when our people found out --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Excuse me, what hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Zenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Very well. I would like now to move on to the conditions in the cells. How much food did you receive there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were in the cells, we received food regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Where did you take your meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Sitting or standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sitting down, at a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: How was the hygiene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a toilet there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were you prevented from going to relieve yourselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were you able to wash up, wash your hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Could you perform religious rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Were you ever present when anybody was mistreated, when anybody was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: In the end, when you were exchanged, was the director present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Did you greet each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We shook hands. Everybody shook hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Does the name Sehovic mean anything to you? He is a merchant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Apparently he was exchanged at the same time when you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is probably the man who was among us in these six vehicles. He is probably their in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: I think that is who you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is who I have in mind. He was there and he was released with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: It was another prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a civilian imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Whose in-law was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, the six of us who went to get that merchandise, he was, sort of, our escort and our guide and in charge of -- for getting this merchandise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know whether this Sehovic, during the release, was taking some things to the director's mother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Someone hit you in your eye. You said he was an HVO soldier. After that, a guard came to ask you about that. Which was the difference between a soldier and a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not after that. That could have been a day or two later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: What I want to know is: which was the difference between a soldier and a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was absolutely no difference. They all wore camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia, and this turnkey who was there, I do not know if he was wounded, but he had it in a sling or something, so he was the guard of our cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We have no more questions for you, sir. Thank you for coming. We wish you a safe journey home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you please bring down the curtains?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
