utterances.text: My learned friend will be taking the next witness, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Is he also a protected witness, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No, your Honour, he is not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, we should open the curtains and everything else. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can I ask your Honour's kindness, how many minutes I have left to start examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, we can begin, but we plan to end at 5.30. That is the usual time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you for your concern, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I am sorry, I was wrong in thinking that the court would be sitting until 5.00. 5.30 is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: There is no problem. I make mistakes too. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are going to read the statement given to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you for coming. You are now going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. MEHO SIVRO

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sivro, do you feel comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Is it all right with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can we start by stating your name, age, date and place of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Meho Sivro. I was born on 15th October 1946 in Sivrino Selo, in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What is your nationality and faith, religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Muslim. My religion is Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Would you please outline briefly for the court which kind of education you did have, which schools did you attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed the technical school in Zenica for metals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you perform any military service and, if so, in which army and with which ranks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I served in the JNA. Upon release, I was a sergeant, a reserve sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Would you please give us a summary of your professional experiences after that, after you completed your studies. In which fields, which tasks and responsibilities, in which factories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I completed technical school, I worked in the corporation called Bratstvo and I was involved in the various jobs. Towards the end I was the co-ordinator of a group for mechanical research.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where is Bratstvo factory located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in Novi Travnik, maybe 500 metres beyond Novi Travnik in the direction of the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What do they produce there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several plants; a plant of castings, then a plant for hydraulics, a plant for tractors and a special purpose factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did they produce military -- any weapons there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what is implied when we talk of special purpose factory. It is weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Which was the proportion between Croats and Muslims employees and workers there at Bratstvo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the actual conflict, which means about 12th April, we got on very well together. But already then, the Muslims were corrected in the way they spoke, they had to use Croat terms, and similar provocations of that kind. Also, they had already loaded weapons and taken them away, but the other side was not allowed to do that because the managers, the sales managers were Croats, who enabled this to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How was the situation in your village, which I understand to be Sivrino Selo, as to the relations between the two groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is called Sivrino Selo. Between the Muslims and the Croats in the area I lived in, Sivrino Selo leans partly on to Dubravice and I was very close with a Croat there, whose nephew is here in the Tribunal, he is called Furundzija, so you know him, and I would go there every week for a party and he would come to visit me. We would talk, have drinks and we were really very close. The other women would come to visit the our women and we would exchange visits. Our relations were very good, even when I was captured. I think that this friend of mine wanted to help me and save me from the camp, but he did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivro. Can you tell the court what happened to you on April 14th 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 13th April I was not working because the situation had deteriorated and in the evening, about seven o'clock, a colleague of mine called me up, a Croat who used to work with me and said: "The situation has settled down and we can go to work". I believed him. However, in the settlement of Stojkovici, we were stopped by the HVO police. I am not sure whether it was the HVO army. Anyway, we were stopped. We all had to show our IDs. Of course, the Muslims were separated to one side, the Croats to the other and I was among those who were separated and transferred to a nearby warehouse in Stojkovici which we are familiar with and we called it Kace. That is where I was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you please explain, by which means were you travelling when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every morning I went on foot for a kilometre from my village where the factory bus would come to pick us up and transfer us every day from Vitez, the railway station at Vitez to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So the Croat which were travelling on the bus were able to reach the factory, they were allowed to go on, on their way to Bratstvo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. They were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And where were you taken from, from there? You say the same of the place --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean from the bus or from the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No, from the place where you were arrested. You were taken to the camp. Which was the camp? Was it a military camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, it was a military warehouse. Since, they had already occupied it as their own, taken possession of it as a military warehouse, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How -- did you recognise the soldiers or the policemen who did arrest you and those who were at the camp? If they were HVO, what kind of insignia did they have and how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms with HVO insignia but I did not recognise any one of those who arrested me. I only recognised a soldier in the camp. I would rather not mention his name for safety reasons, but I think his name is mentioned in my statement. He is a very well-known figure in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You mean his safety, not your safety, I imagine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My own. My safety. I am thinking of my own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you find other persons detained on your arrival at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. But there were not many of them because I came there early, about 6.30. I did not look at my watch, so I do not know exactly, but as time went by more and more of them came so that by the evening on that day, there were about 50 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were they all Muslims, were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were, but not necessarily. There may have been a Serb among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: But anyway, they were all civilians, there were no soldiers among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about their average age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think between 18 and close to 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So at the end of the day, how many of them did spend the night in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us. We all spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Yes, but how many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fifty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Then what happened the day after? You spent all the day after at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We spent the whole day in a very crowded container. There were a lot of us there. The container was small, so that in the evening -- I think this was after midnight -- we were transferred by bus to Busovaca. Seven of those people were released to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: From Busovaca, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken from the camp to dig trenches in the village of Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: After you left the camp and by bus, you said you were taken to Busovaca. Would you be more precise about that, in Busovaca or near Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp in Busovaca, it is called Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: When did you arrive at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was after midnight. I think it was about 1.00 am, 10 or 15 minutes after 1.00. They took all our watches away. But anyway, it was after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was it April 15th, the night --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If it was after midnight, then this was the 16th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So you arrived that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sivro, I am going to show you an aerial photograph of the camp. Can it be introduced as usual? Can it be numbered? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Will you put, please, the photograph on the ELMO, Mr. Usher? So, Mr. Sivro, can you look at the photograph on your right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So you said you arrived that night. Do you remember passing through a gate on entering the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. We passed through the gate. We hardly stopped there at all and we reached a warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you show us where that warehouse is on the map -- on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. (Indicating on photograph). It is this one, this building here. This warehouse I am showing you with the stick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you mark it with the pen and put on it the letter "A", please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph). I have marked the part in front of the building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Usher, could you please help the witness with his headphones, so that he can listen in comfort.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is fine now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us from the bus were put up in this hangar. Of course, we had to immediately line up against the wall with our hands up and without saying anything at all or without moving. We had to stand there for almost two hours, for roughly two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you searched by the guards or the soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They ordered us to take out everything we had in our pockets; money, everything we had. They threatened if anyone did not do as they were told, that they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you have any money with you, or other personal belongings that you had to give to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had some money. I had a watch, a pen knife and a pencil. They took all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you have rings on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said I had my wedding ring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So, did you have to give it to the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to put it aside. Of course, they took it for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: When you say "they", you mean HVO soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How were they dressing? How did you recognise them as HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms. I did not see the HVO insignia because we did not dare look at those soldiers. We had to turn our heads towards the wall with our hands up. One of the soldiers shouted so much at us that we did not dare move an inch, not to mention turning our heads around to see -- at least I did not see. I saw they were in camouflage uniforms, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were there any other prisoners in the hangar when you did arrive there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were. I think about 80 to 100 prisoners were already there in the hangar. They were almost all of them lined up against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you, were you registered or were your names taken down and written down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some soldiers at a table and we moved one by one and they registered us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who did register you? Who did take your names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers, but I do not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: In that occasion, were you given an opportunity to meet with the camp commander or warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not, but this soldier who was shouting at us, he said, like this: "Whoever moves, don't you dare move, because our commander is here. You have to be quiet". However, one of those in the previous group must have been on good relations with this soldier and he asked: "Who was the commander", all he answered, he was a fat man from Loncari, he just said "Aleksovski". I remember that name because it is a strange surname for us, it is usually a Macedonian surname. That is how it stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: In saying that, did he point to somebody who was present in the hangar and was then supposed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you describe more in detail, to whom you did give your name? Have you been -- did somebody interrogate you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, two soldiers were sitting there, one was writing things down, the other one was watching. They wrote down our names, first names, where we came from and that sort of thing. There was a great deal of fear amongst us so I do not remember very well all the things he asked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was the man who has been indicated as the commander sitting behind his desk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought it was the commander, the one who was not writing down anything. I thought he must be the man in charge, so I did look at him a little. He seemed to me to be fair, rather balding. I personally thought that he was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You do not think, or do you think you would be able to recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You have never had any other occasion to meet with the camp commander during those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have met him, but I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long were you forced to stay in the hangar in that position, with your hands up and facing the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think for more than two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Then did you spend the night there in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We spent it in the hangar in a corner, on the concrete. It was cold. I was not dressed very well, so I was freezing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you given food and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing until the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day they immediately took about 20 men somewhere, but when they came back, they told us they went to dig trenches, because we did not know where they were taking them. Anyway, it was in the area of Bare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who called the prisoners off in order to send them trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The names were called out by a soldier, a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You mean an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did he read the names out of a list or just did he choose the prisoners at random?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time he read out the names and then the following days he did not read the names, he selected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So, how long did you have to work trench digging that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go to trench digging that day, but they went and they came back in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did all of them come back? Did all of those who had been chosen come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that first day, I am not sure that they all returned, but the following days all of them did not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You mean not all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How many were missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I do not know. But the following days, every time they came back someone was missing. They said they were killed by a BiH army sniper or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And how did the prisoners who had returned to the camp explain the fact that some of their fellows were missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They knew by name who was missing, so they would say, for instance, "those two were wounded and were transferred to the hospital at Nova Bila", so we thought that they were, indeed, transferred to Nova Bila; however, they are missing to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, let us go to your personal experience. How many times were you taken trench digging during your stay at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where were you taken the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the village of Jelinak both times, both the first and the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: May I introduce in evidence the map you already know, of the area, please? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sivro, would you please sign on the map the locations where you have been taken trench digging with the pen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Shall I mark it with the marker?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Yes, mark it, please. While digging, or anyway working, were you exposed to fire from the opposing lines in the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the first day while I was digging, we were led by a guard, an HVO soldier, through a clearing where five or six of us -- all of us could have got killed because a burst of fire was opened on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Tell us about the second time you were taken trench digging. You said it was the same area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same village. On that day too, when we were in that village, the village was still burning. Some explosions could be heard. They said that they were bombs left behind by the Muslims, but it was obvious that it was the tiles or the concrete that was exploding. I was close to a garage that was burning and there was coal inside. The concrete was red hot and obviously it was cracking too. They said that these were bombs that had been left behind by the Muslims. I mean the HVO soldiers said that, that these were bombs and ammunition left behind. The second time when I came to dig trenches it was during the night shift -- it was already dark, I do not exactly know what time it was -- until morning. If you want me to tell you all the details, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Yes, tell us the details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got to the village of Jelinak on board of a truck, there were about 20 to 25 of us. We got off and then each of the guards or the soldiers would take two to three of us, as many as he needed. My task was to dig trenches at the end of the village, together with another colleague, along a river. They told us not to dig a real trench, but like a hole, three by two metres and, with another tall man, I only know his first name -- so that we dug all night. In the morning, maybe about 5.00 roughly, the BiH army started shelling the village. The Croats, the HVO, were prepared for defence, as if they knew, and they said that they knew that the BiH army would attack that morning. They were shelling. However, close to me not a single shell fell, but we asked if we could at least stop working so as to avoid being hit. However, they would not let us stop working, we had to go on digging. In the morning, the attack started. The BiH army, we heard when they had brought what we call a tekbijr. Panic started amongst the HVO soldiers. We were afraid too because if they came there, they would probably think that we were soldiers too and shoot us. So a guard who was responsible for us, he asked one of the commanders there: "What should I do with the prisoners?" Just then, another two arrived, probably from the nearby trenches. They were also digging. They joined us. I was the last to come out of this dug-out. Then the commander said that he should take us to Loncari and kill us all. I got frightened, of course. I thought it was the end, that we would all be executed and he took us through the village, the four of us. However, towards the end of the village of Jelinak a man stopped us and he asked this soldier who was escorting us what was his password. He sort of mumbled or he did not know, and he said that we should not be taken anywhere but executed right there next to a house: "Why should you waste time taking them anywhere else?" This house is not on the road, but it is slightly uphill and we reached that house and face turned towards the wall. But this man who was escorting us did not want to kill us there. However, from that house, a fat man emerged and he would not let him kill us. They quarrelled for about 10 minutes and then he ordered that we turn around. I am not sure whether it was this same man that gave the order because we were facing the wall. When we turned around, perhaps their command was there. Anyway, they apparently agreed not to kill us. He offered us cigarettes. I do not smoke. We asked for water. We were given water. We were there for about 10 minutes. Anyway, we were terrified. We thought that death was inevitable. One of us four -- I do not remember exactly who it was -- he said to the rest of us to pray to God: "This is the end", and that is what we believed. However, the one who brought us there said we were going on. Since I had heard the previous order given to him, I kept thinking of how I could get out of this situation and a chance occurred --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you at this point, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I think that -- it will probably -- I would like for him to go into details as to his personal experience and I would not like to hurry him up. I hope your Honours will understand. It is not an easy story, even though it is short in terms of time, but I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, we understand very well. I should like to say to the witness that we have to adjourn for the moment. Therefore, tomorrow, we will meet again here. I think it is 5.30 and it is time for us to adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: on Wednesday, 4th March 1998)
